description_full: Tyler Technologies, Inc. provides integrated software and technology management solutions for the public sector in the United States. It operates in two segments, Enterprise Software and Platform Technologies. The company designs, develops, markets, and supports a range of software solutions to serve mission-critical back-office functions. It also offers platform and transformative technology solutions, such as cybersecurity services, including threat detection, response, vulnerability testing, and security training, data and insights, digital solutions, payments, platform technologies, and outdoor recreation solutions; public administration solutions, including civic services, ERP, property and recording, and regulatory; and corrections, courts and justice, and public safety solutions. In addition, the company provides school ERP and student transportation K-12 education solutions; and health and human services solutions comprising environmental health, and disability and benefits. It has a strategic collaboration agreement with Amazon Web Services for cloud hosting services. The company was formerly known as Tyler Corporation and changed its name to Tyler Technologies, Inc. in June 1999. Tyler Technologies, Inc. was founded in 1966 and is based in Plano, Texas.

financial_summary: Tyler Technologies, Inc. is a large-cap technology business with a $16.8B market cap on $2.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +15% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 46%.

The business throws off $638M in free cash flow — roughly 27 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.07× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 72× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 1.0%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 15% operating margin runs 9pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.66x).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 536 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 19% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 14% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 42% and a beta of 0.94, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.28 vs 5y 0.92), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $245.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 23% in the 2020 crash, 45% in the 2022 bear market and 36% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $286 (margin of safety -48%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 29%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $152 to $558 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 52.7 vs 25.8 and EV/EBITDA 36.4 vs 16.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 30% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 22 covering analysts target $450 on average, 7% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.66).
It runs a 46% gross margin and converts 27% of revenue into free cash flow, or 21% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 2.07x.
ROE of 9% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 6.5% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $497.5M (3% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.4, in the safe zone).
Goodwill makes up 46% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.0% over 3 years, 15.9% over 5 years and 14.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 13.9% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.07 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 1.0x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 11%.
Capex runs only 0.1x depreciation (0.7% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 37, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.5%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (30 sales, net $37.3M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.0% (1.0% in buybacks).
people: With about 7,972 employees, each generates about $293K of revenue, 0.8x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 15.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $80K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $685K (2x revenue per employee).
